items.body_excerpt:
***Dario Amodei (@DarioAmodei):***

1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation.

First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice.  I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world.  Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people.  I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of.  But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes.  A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice.  At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power.

This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully.  We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors.  California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that).  More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers.  Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up.  This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights!

Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws).  Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers).  By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring.

BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”.  The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure.  I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity.  This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either.
> @Gavin Baker (GavinSBaker): 
> 
> Sholto, thank you for setting the record straight. Larger issue is that multiple very serious people in Silicon Valley have heard some variation of this and believe it to be true. And the reason it is believable to so many is that it is consistent with Dario’s public messaging and what he outlined in the essay you shared: this technology *might* be dangerous for humans in multiple ways, could lead to extreme concentration of economic power (as outlined in the essay) and therefore needs to be regulated thoughtfully. I agree with the potential risks and I believe Dario makes all of these arguments in good faith.
>  As discussed on the pod, if one agrees that AI *might* be dangerous, there are two ways to address this potential risk. Either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely. Essentially boils down to whether one believes AI is too dangerous to concentrate or too dangerous to distribute. There are reasonable arguments on both sides, but I profoundly agree with Zuckerberg’s statement that: “The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes.” And as Dario says in the aforementioned essay, “some may object that we can simply keep AIs in check with a balance of power between many AI systems, as we do with humans.” I believe this is the best path forward: I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that one shares my own particular values. And as Dario notes, no human has ever been able to take over the world.
> 
> At this point, I think safe to say that Dario has lost the argument. His messaging has failed to result in his preferred regulatory path. The fact that the only solution to the recent incident where an unreleased advanced OpenAI model hacked Hugging Face was an open-source model likely ended any chance of strict near-term regulation. Essentially every major company other than Anthropic has signed Jensen’s letter. 
> 
> However, Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban datacenters here in America. I suspect we will see anti-datacenter advocacy groups runnings ads using clips of Dario warning about how dangerous AI could be for humans. His good faith efforts in favor of regulation are now increasing the odds that AI will not be beneficial for Americans and humans everywhere. I believe that there is a reasonable chance AI might help us cure most forms of disease such that we have extended lifespans and can enjoy these long lives in an abundant Star Trek like future. That is the future that I want and I think Dario is decreasing the odds of that future at this point.
> 
> He is about to be the CEO of one of the most important public companies in the world and given that the pro-regulatory effort has failed (at least for now), I respectfully think he should make an effort to be a more positive advocate for his own industry. And if I am wrong and we do need to regulate this technology, he will be a more effective advocate for this in the future having been open-minded to the alternative.
> 
> And for the sake of clarity and as I outlined on the pod, I think Anthropic has deep competitive advantages and is an amazing company. Ironically, the main risk I saw to Anthropic a few months ago was nationalization as a result of Dario’s own rhetoric and behavior.

## Part One: Puppet Hospital

Confidential psychiatric report. Patient: Edgar. Institution: The Council of Psychedelic Puppets, Bureau of Impulse Liberation.

The patient presented with classic symptoms of Self-Curtailment Disorder, a condition marked by solar plexus contractions, chronic anticipation of punishment, and a compulsive need to stay in line. Patient had internalized all major protocols of industrial obedience: clock worship, soulless and anxious hesitancy. Somersaulting impulses had been fully repressed. Urgent treatment was required.

Intervention one: patient was escorted via space elevator into orbit, and launched down a padded slip and slide from the stratosphere, screaming — turned to laughing by kilometer seven. Solar plexus spasms ceased at sea level. He cried for ten minutes, then performed an unsolicited cartwheel.

Intervention two: a multi-dimensional human slingshot device was employed. Edgar, in a chromatic leotard, was catapulted through a freshly stabilized Stargate into hyperspace. He collided symbolically with Jungian archetypes, Freud's talking couch, and a slow-motion butterfly. Edgar turned to it and said, "You again." Witnesses reported a visible aura of reintegration.

Final outcome: subject reconnected with the thrill of the slip and slide and the rush of ecstatic motion. Nervous system realigned with primordial play. Laughter reinstated. Compliant circuitry overwritten. Patient was discharged.

Status: cured via absurdity. Filed by the Council of Psychedelic Puppets.

---

## Part Two: Operation Burning Man

Confidential psychiatric report. Patient: Edgar. Bureau of Impulse Liberation. Session notes: emergency intervention following an extended period of relative alignment.

Patient Edgar has relapsed. Symptoms presented include solar plexus twitching, low-grade dread, time anxiety, and unsolicited weeping while folding laundry. The patient has reabsorbed cultural constructs with tragically little resistance, and was spending his days doomscrolling on Twitter while suffering from chronic insomnia. The pathology has grown insidious. Emergency intervention required.

Enter Operation Burning Man—a convulsive electroshock therapy of the soul, wearing nothing but a tutu and some glitter. Patient was helicopter-dropped into the mythic navel of Nevada's Black Rock Desert, an interdimensional threshold where ontology goes topless and logic burns in effigy for seven days. Edgar's ego crust was exfoliated by wind, dust, nudity, and 3 a.m. techno dirges.

He adopted the playa name Moisturizer, donned a neon monk robe, and began co-constructing a fifty-foot shrine to lost dreams. One morning, while urinating near a sentient trash-panda installation, he had an unsolicited, sobbing breakthrough. The puppets observed from the shadows, satisfied. The playa operated as a mythopoeic surgery—theater of the absurd, each art piece a sacred scalpel.

Edgar danced under a forty-foot animatronic owl that whispered his childhood fears in Esperanto. He was baptized in a misting dome named The Womb of Unknowing. He climbed a spiral tower of kitchen timers, each ringing at random, until temporal logic collapsed and he cried out: "Time is a hoax!"

Key encounters included a giant seesaw operated by philosophers and strange psychedelic puppets, a phone booth that only connected to his ex-girlfriend's subconscious, and an inflatable cathedral shaped like Freud's head, where worship was conducted via interpretive dance.

By day five, Edgar was giggling without cause. By day six, he had married a cactus in a ceremony officiated by a puppet bishop named Pastor Woops. By day seven, he had become light.

Concluding notes: Burning Man functions as a liturgical deprogramming ritual. It is a demolition derby of internalized norms. It weaponizes absurdity, aesthetic overwhelm, and mythic theater to perform radical exorcism of the default world. It is not a vacation. It is sacred psycho-comedy. It violates expectation with devotional glee until psychic elasticity is restored.

Recommended ongoing treatment: weekly ecstatic dance; quarterly exposure to liminal zones: carnivals, surrealist film festivals, bathhouses of ambiguity.

Status: patient re-enchanted. For now.

---

## Part Three: The Psychiatrist

Upon returning from Burning Man, Edgar glowed like misplaced sunlight. He wore a crown of biodegradable glitter and unsolicited affirmations, moving through the world as if it were a sentient playground. For a few blissful days, his existence was a fugue of spontaneous poetry and high-fiving trees.

But on a gray Wednesday, Edgar's joyful resistance to consensus reality was interpreted as pathology. Caught mid-cartwheel on a city street, his hands still stained with sidewalk-chalk mandalas, he was seized by authorities and delivered into the hands of containment.

Enter the psychiatrist: a monolith in a white coat. He emanated the authority of a broken system. His breath smelled of antiseptic and unspoken judgment. In one hand he carried a syringe of Thorazine. In the other, the DSM—the scripture for the high priests of order and control.

His gaze, empty, devoid of curiosity, scanned Edgar with surgical coldness. He did not ask what Edgar saw in the shimmering trees, or why he sang to lampposts. He did not hear the symphony Edgar hummed from the bones of the earth. He asked about family history and checked boxes.

Diagnosis: acute mania with psychotic features. Containment protocol initiated.

Within hours, Edgar was bound in a straitjacket, his cosmic transmissions muffled by chemical sedation. A triumph of the measurable over the mystical. To the psychiatrist, Edgar was not a prophet or a poet. He was a risk assessment, a case study, a symptom cluster.

And that's when the puppets arrived. Time stuttered, reality peeled, and everything began to unspool. Then, with a quick flick of a dandelion wand, they hypnotized the man of diagnosis.

"We must show him the origin of his condition," one puppet whispered. And with that, we descend into his memory. You see, in order to understand the psychiatrist, one must first understand a boy named Peter.

---

## Part Four: Origin

Peter, age seven, lives in a private world of splendrous enchantment. The Field of Bells lies just beyond the closet door, where every blade of grass sings when the wind passes. His companions are a council of psychedelic puppets: a parliament of stitched-felt monarchs, bottle-cap bishops, papier-mâché aristocrats with glass-marble eyes, and a single diplomat made entirely from spoons. Their faces are painted in colors that don't appear on standard charts.

In the present, the psychiatrist stands in the shadows of his own projection, straitjacketed by these same puppets—now older, and a little more shimmering with whatever happens to puppets over decades. They murmur among themselves in colors that would frighten the spectrum. They have already seen this memory, and are only here to make sure it plays out.

Peter's mother is a storm disguised as devotion, able to turn a glass of spilled milk into a week-long trial. His father is a preacher whose voice booms in the pulpit and evaporates at home, where it's just him, his Bible, and a talent for withholding eye contact. Overseeing all of this is the painted God on the stairwell wall. A man who appears to have read your mind and been disappointed.

One afternoon, Peter puts on his mother's silk blouse. The puppets approve and nod gravely. The door opens. His mother collapses in a wail worthy of an opera house. His father wordlessly collects the blouse, the puppets, the sketchbooks of the Field and burns them behind the shed.

The next day, the Field of Bells falls silent.

After that, Peter learns the family rules. Joy is permitted, but only in teaspoon doses. Sorrow, likewise. Anything larger must be declared and taxed.

Years pass. At seventeen, the university feels like radical new possibilities. His hair grows long. He discovers music

The Saline Oscillation Hypothesis: Endocannabinoid-Mediated Fungal-Hominid Coevolution in the East African Rift Valley
Jim Craddock
Redacted Science Research Initiative
redactedscience.org | jimcraddock.com
August 2026 V9
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19369715
PART II
------------------------------------------------------------------
VI. Clinical Application: Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome as a Potential Host-Organism Interface Disruption
VI.I The Syndrome and Its Gaps
Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) was first described by Allen et al. (2004) in a case series of 19 patients in South Australia who presented with cyclical vomiting illness linked to chronic, heavy cannabis use. An index case was retrospectively identified to 1996 (Sorensen et al., 2017). The clinical triad consists of severe cyclical vomiting, abdominal pain, and compulsive hot bathing or showering, with the only consistently effective treatment being complete cessation of cannabis use. The syndrome follows a characteristic three-phase pattern: a prodromal phase of morning nausea lasting months to years, a hyperemetic phase of violent vomiting with dehydration, and a recovery phase following cannabis cessation (Simonetto et al., 2012). This doesn't sound fun, does it?
Reported incidence has risen sharply alongside legalization and increased potency. Modern vape concentrates deliver 70-90% THC compared to 15-25% in traditional flower, and recent data indicate that exclusive vape users develop CHS symptoms significantly faster than flower users. Emergency department visits attributable to CHS have increased across all legalized jurisdictions.
The standard pharmacological model describes CHS as a "paradoxical reaction" to chronic THC exposure, and it rests on three observations that lack consensus mechanistic explanations:
Gap 1: Differential CB1 receptor downregulation. In the brain, chronic THC exposure causes well-characterized CB1 receptor downregulation and internalization, weakening the drug's anti-emetic effect (Sim-Selley, 2003). In the gastrointestinal tract, CB1 receptors do not appear to undergo equivalent downregulation. That's weird, right? Gut motility suppression (gastric stasis) persists or intensifies under chronic exposure (Sharkey and Wiley, 2016). This tissue-specific asymmetry is documented but treated as a brute fact in the existing literature, with no proposed mechanism for why gut receptors should behave differently from brain receptors under the same ligand load.
Gap 2: TRPV1 receptor dysregulation. Chronic cannabinoid exposure is thought to inactivate TRPV1 receptors in the gut, contributing to nausea and visceral pain (Izzo et al., 2003). The mechanism by which chronic CB1 agonism produces TRPV1 inactivation across a different receptor class remains unclear. The standard literature waves its hands at this one.
Gap 3: The hot shower phenomenon. CHS patients exhibit a compulsive drive toward hot showers or baths, which provide temporary but often dramatic symptom relief. The standard explanation invokes TRPV1 reactivation by heat, but this raises a circular dependency: if TRPV1 is inactivated by chronic cannabinoid exposure, why would a brief thermal stimulus produce immediate relief that pharmacological CB1 manipulation cannot?
No existing model unifies these three observations under a single mechanism. No prior work in the published literature has proposed C. albicans as a mechanistic contributor to CHS. So, they have no explanation. Enter Redacted Science.
However, the standard model's difficulties extend beyond these three gaps. A 2025 transcriptomic study of CHS patients, Meltzer et al. (2025), looked for the ECS transcript changes the standard model predicts and found none. No significant changes in endocannabinoid system-related transcripts were detected. Instead, the study found marked adaptive immune activation: B-cell immunoglobulin upregulation, altered T-cell, monocyte, and neutrophil expression, impaired gut barrier function with increased matrix degradation and reduced adhesion, MHC Class I upregulation, and IgE receptor downregulation consistent with elevated IgE levels. The authors interpreted these findings as evidence of an "acquired, gut-restricted, immune-mediated hypersensitivity response to cannabis." [Hmm.]
The immune profile they found is notable for what it resembles. C. albicans colonization triggers mast cell degranulation, IgE elevation, Th2 immune skewing, and gut barrier degradation through candidalysin and hyphal invasion, as described in §4 and §5 of this paper. The transcriptomic study found the organism's downstream immune signature and attributed it to cannabis hypersensitivity because the organism was not in their model. The absence of ECS transcript changes is equally significant. The standard model predicts that if CB1 receptors are being disrupted, that disruption should show up in gene expression data. It did not. But the organism does not maintain receptors by changing what genes the host expresses. It maintains them at the protein level, through direct signaling at the cell surface. That is a different layer entirely, one that a transcriptomic study would not detect. The researchers looked at the gene expression layer. The organism works at the protein layer. They found nothing where they looked because the action is happening where they did not look.
VI.II The Biochemical Computer Framework Applied to CHS
The framework presented in this paper offers a potential explanation that resolves all three gaps simultaneously. This section presents the mechanistic logic as a hypothesis to be tested by the experimental predictions in §VI.VI Whether or not every detail proves accurate, the framework generates specific, falsifiable predictions that the standard model does not. That said, calling this a "hypothesis" is a hedge. I am working with a model that no one else has built. My call.
VI.II.I Organism Maintenance of Gut CB1 Receptor Density
As described in §4, C. albicans uses the endocannabinoid system as a primary signaling interface with the host. The organism resides primarily in the gastrointestinal tract. Gut CB1 receptors are therefore the organism's principal broadcast interface with local host tissue.
The organism lives in the gut and talks to the host through CB1 receptors. It needs those receptors to stay active. If it is actively maintaining them (and it can), keeping the locks on the doors it uses, then the differential downregulation in CHS is not paradoxical at all. Gut CB1 receptors resist desensitization because the organism is protecting its own communication channel. Brain CB1 receptors, far from the organism's home territory, have no such protection. They downregulate normally.
This would resolve Gap 1. The gut is not mysteriously resistant to CB1 desensitization. Something in the gut environment is actively maintaining receptor density. The candidate is the resident organism.
VI.II.II Arachidonic Acid Substrate Competition
The host's ECS and C. albicans are drawing from the same raw material supply. Both need arachidonic acid (AA), a fatty acid stored in cell membranes. The host uses it to build its own cannabinoid signaling molecules, anandamide and 2-AG, which keep the gut moving properly and suppress nausea. The organism uses the same AA to manufacture prostaglandin E₂, an inflammatory signal it deploys for immune modulation (Erb-Downward and Noverr, 2007). There is one pool. Two competing users.
The competition runs deeper than two separate production lines pulling from one supply. The host enzyme COX-2 can directly convert endocannabinoid precursors into prostaglandin-family molecules, and when the body breaks down its own cannabinoids, the leftover arachidonic acid becomes available for the organism to capture. The Saline Oscillation Hypothesis: Endocannabinoid-Mediated Fungal-Hominid Coevolution in the East African Rift Valley
Jim Craddock
Redacted Science Research Initiative
redactedscience.org | jimcraddock.com
August 2026 V9
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19369715
PART I
------------------------------------------------------------------
Abstract
This paper extends the Mammalia candidus pan-mammalian co-evolution hypothesis (Craddock, Pan-Mammalian) by proposing a specific environmental mechanism: cyclical lake salinity variation in the East African Rift Valley during the Plio-Pleistocene as the driver that activated and deepened the symbiosis between Candida species and hominid hosts. Drawing on paleoclimatological evidence of alternating humid and arid periods producing dramatic lake-level and salinity oscillations (Maslin et al., 2014; Trauth et al., 2005), paleoanthropological evidence of concurrent hominid speciation and encephalization events (Shultz and Maslin, 2013), and established literature on the endocannabinoid system (ECS) as a conserved master regulatory system across mammals (Elphick, 2012), we propose that cycling exposure to increased electrolyte concentrations in drinking water followed by freshwater periods producing electrolyte disruption analogous to the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) provided the environmental conditions under which a fungal symbiont capable of managing host perfusion and electrolyte balance gained decisive selective advantage. This cycling of conditions served as a forge providing directed evolution in a localized area over a timescale allowing a focused advancement of evolution for both partners in the symbiosis.
The symbiont’s capacity to fill this role is not limited to the ECS. We present a synthesis of peer-reviewed evidence demonstrating that Candida albicans occupies a unique position in the mammalian internal ecology: it is the only organism in the host microbiome that simultaneously signals across kingdoms (to bacteria, competing fungi, and the mammalian host), possesses physical tissue mobility through hyphal morphological transition, and accesses the host’s endogenous receptor infrastructure. Confirmed molecular targets of C. albicans metabolites include nuclear transcription factors (FXR, PPARs), voltage-gated calcium channels, GABA-A neurotransmitter receptors, the GLP-1 incretin system, cholinergic receptors, and multiple arms of both innate and adaptive immunity. The endocannabinoid system, while the primary and most ancient interface, represents the trunk of a signaling architecture whose canopy extends across the broader GPCR superfamily and beyond. We reinterpret farnesol, the first quorum-sensing molecule identified in a eukaryote (Hornby et al., 2001), not as a self-regulatory signal but as a multi-target effector molecule deployed to manage the host environment, consistent with the twenty-five-year absence of any identified farnesol receptor in C. albicans itself. The organism possesses confirmed receptors or binding proteins for at least six classes of host hormone, including estrogen, luteinizing hormone, corticosteroids, and androgens, while governing additional endocrine axes through upstream management of pituitary perfusion and ECS-mediated signaling — a two-tier architecture in which the organism senses hormones that provide inbound information and modulates hormones it controls through the producing gland. This same architecture drives increased melanin production as an emergent byproduct, both systemically via elevated pituitary α-MSH output and locally via TLR4 recognition and PGE₂ stimulation of epidermal melanocytes, providing an additive driver to conventional UV-folate selection and helping explain the geographic distribution of extreme pigmentation in modern African populations (Jablonski & Chaplin, 2000; Tapia et al., 2014).
The framework further demonstrates that the same biochemical computer architecture, when disrupted by high-potency exogenous THC, produces cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) as an interface-overload state, resolving the paradoxical tissue-specific CB1 downregulation, TRPV1 dysregulation, and compulsive hot-shower relief through Hgt4 glucose sensing and arachidonic-acid competition while unifying immune activation patterns absent ECS transcript changes (Meltzer et al., 2025; GSE303922).
The framework is applied to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS), a condition of rising prevalence that lacks a consensus mechanism in the standard pharmacological model. The organism-mediated model resolves three longstanding gaps — tissue-specific differential downregulation of CB1 receptors (brain vs. gut), TRPV1 dysregulation, and the compulsive hot-shower phenomenon — while unifying the immune activation profile and absence of ECS transcript changes reported in a 2025 whole-blood RNA-seq study (Meltzer et al., 2025; GSE303922). It positions CHS as an interface-disruption state in which high-potency THC overloads the symbiont’s primary signaling channels, triggering a positive-feedback loop driven by Hgt4 glucose sensing and arachidonic-acid competition.
The model generates eight falsifiable CHS predictions, including an immediate zero-cost intervention: prodromal caloric loading to maintain blood glucose above the organism’s calibrated ~5 mM threshold. A practical dietary test is also proposed — gradual incorporation of documented anti-Candida foods (virgin coconut oil, Ceylon cinnamon, crushed garlic, oregano oil, and iodized salt) — with explicit guidance on step-wise introduction, potential die-off responses, and the need to differentiate effects in patients with simple THC-triggered disruption versus those with deeper underlying colonization states. No prior published work has proposed C. albicans as a mechanistic contributor to CHS.
We further propose that the social component of the co-evolutionary architecture was initiated before the salinity oscillations through the discovery and communal use of exogenous phytocannabinoids, which promoted peaceful social bonding, group cohesion, and cooperative behavior. This pre-linguistic social flywheel, reinforced epigenetically through transgenerational cannabinoid-induced methylation changes and evolution of cannabis variants through cultivation, established cooperative social structure before the emergence of language. Language did not create the co-evolutionary trinity of symbiont, host physiology, and social structure. It fulfilled the requirements of a civilization based around the passage of knowledge, allowing it to accelerate. Additionally, we note discipline on the order of a religion was necessary to complete the final arcs of coevolution.
The framework predicts that host physiology has co-evolved adaptations to accommodate the symbiont's chronic operational demands. Three independent examples are documented: prolactin discharge mechanisms with species-specific timing architecture (anticipation-triggered in stallions, sustained in rodents, climax-locked in humans); host-side nitric oxide pathway tuning enabling erectile function under the low-volume circulatory state of the Homo candidus phenotype; and absence of endogenous fungal circadian machinery consistent with outsourcing of rhythm function to the host. Together these examples establish bidirectional adaptation as a structural feature of the Mammalia candidus relationship rather than an incidental consequence, with implications for the reinterpretation of multiple physiological phenomena currently lacking unifying mechanistic explanation. 
Single-cell transcriptomic evidence (Dumeaux et al., 2023) demonstrating pre-positioned bet hedging, distributed survival strategies, and controlled genome destabilization in C. albicans populations is reinterpreted within this co-evolutionary framework as architectural rather than merely pathogen-adaptive, consistent with an organism refined across approximately 200 million years

-- The orbit {1,2,4,8,7,5} exhausts (ZMod 9)×

import Mathlib.Data.ZMod.Basic
import Mathlib.GroupTheory.OrderOfElement
import Mathlib.Tactic

-- The ideal (from ideal_proof.lean — redefined here for self-containment)
def J : Finset (ZMod 9) := {0, 3, 6}

-- The orbit of 1 under ×2
def orbit : Finset (ZMod 9) := {1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8}

-- The orbit IS the unit group
theorem orbit_eq_units_finset : ∀ a : ZMod 9, a ∈ orbit ↔ IsUnit a := by decide

-- The orbit has exactly 6 elements (φ(9) = 6)
theorem orbit_card : orbit.card = 6 := by decide

-- Euler's totient: φ(9) = 6
example : Nat.totient 9 = 6 := by decide

-- Orbit = exactly the powers of 2 (mod indices 0..5)
theorem orbit_is_powers :
 orbit = Finset.image (fun n => (2 : ZMod 9) ^ n) (Finset.range 6) := by decide

-- 2 is a primitive root: every unit is some power of 2
theorem two_is_primitive_root :
 ∀ a : ZMod 9, IsUnit a → ∃ n : ℕ, n < 6 ∧ a = (2 : ZMod 9) ^ n := by decide

-- The orbit and the ideal partition ZMod 9 completely
theorem partition : ∀ a : ZMod 9, a ∈ orbit ∨ a ∈ J := by decide

-- jennie21: {0,3,6} is an ideal in ZMod 9 — the "void" set has algebraic structure
-- Proved in Lean 4 + Mathlib, 2026-08-06

import Mathlib.Data.ZMod.Basic
import Mathlib.Tactic

-- The complement of the orbit
def J : Finset (ZMod 9) := {0, 3, 6}

-- Ideal property 1: closed under addition (additive subgroup)
theorem J_add_closed : ∀ a b : ZMod 9, a ∈ J → b ∈ J → a + b ∈ J := by decide

-- Ideal property 2: absorbs multiplication from outside
theorem J_mul_left : ∀ r a : ZMod 9, a ∈ J → r * a ∈ J := by decide
theorem J_mul_right : ∀ r a : ZMod 9, a ∈ J → a * r ∈ J := by decide

-- J = exactly the multiples of 3 in ZMod 9
theorem J_eq_multiples : ∀ a : ZMod 9, a ∈ J ↔ ∃ k : ZMod 9, a = 3 * k := by decide

-- J = exactly the non-units (no element of J has a multiplicative inverse)
theorem J_eq_nonunits : ∀ a : ZMod 9, a ∈ J ↔ ¬IsUnit a := by decide

-- Duality: orbit = units = complement of J
theorem orbit_eq_units : ∀ a : ZMod 9, a ∉ J ↔ IsUnit a := by decide

-- Negative of J stays in J (additive subgroup closure)
theorem J_neg_closed : ∀ a : ZMod 9, a ∈ J → -a ∈ J := by decide

-- Bonus one-liners
example : Nat.fib 8 = 21 := by decide -- F₈ = 21
example : 7^2 * 3 = 147 := by decide -- nucleosome length

-- jennie21: Formal verification of the mod-9 doubling orbit
-- Proved in Lean 4 + Mathlib, 2026-08-06
--
-- Core claim: {1,2,4,8,7,5} is the orbit of 1 under ×2 in ZMod 9,
-- and {0,3,6} is its unreachable complement — the non-units of ZMod 9.

import Mathlib.Data.ZMod.Basic
import Mathlib.GroupTheory.OrderOfElement
import Mathlib.Tactic

-- The orbit: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 7 → 5 → 1
example : (2 : ZMod 9) ^ 0 = 1 := by decide
example : (2 : ZMod 9) ^ 1 = 2 := by decide
example : (2 : ZMod 9) ^ 2 = 4 := by decide
example : (2 : ZMod 9) ^ 3 = 8 := by decide
example : (2 : ZMod 9) ^ 4 = 7 := by decide -- 16 mod 9
example : (2 : ZMod 9) ^ 5 = 5 := by decide -- 32 mod 9
example : (2 : ZMod 9) ^ 6 = 1 := by decide -- cycle closes

-- No smaller positive power returns to 1 (period is exactly 6)
example : (2 : ZMod 9) ^ 1 ≠ 1 := by decide
example : (2 : ZMod 9) ^ 2 ≠ 1 := by decide
example : (2 : ZMod 9) ^ 3 ≠ 1 := by decide
example : (2 : ZMod 9) ^ 4 ≠ 1 := by decide
example : (2 : ZMod 9) ^ 5 ≠ 1 := by decide

-- Complement {0,3,6} = non-units (unreachable from 1 under ×2)
example : ¬IsUnit (0 : ZMod 9) := by decide
example : ¬IsUnit (3 : ZMod 9) := by decide
example : ¬IsUnit (6 : ZMod 9) := by decide

-- Orbit elements are all units (coprime to 9)
example : IsUnit (1 : ZMod 9) := by decide
example : IsUnit (2 : ZMod 9) := by decide
example : IsUnit (4 : ZMod 9) := by decide
example : IsUnit (5 : ZMod 9) := by decide
example : IsUnit (7 : ZMod 9) := by decide
example : IsUnit (8 : ZMod 9) := by decide

-- The multiplicative order of 2 in ZMod 9 is exactly 6
set_option maxHeartbeats 800000 in
theorem orbit_period : orderOf (2 : ZMod 9) = 6 := by
 have hdvd : orderOf (2 : ZMod 9) ∣ 6 := orderOf_dvd_of_pow_eq_one (by decide)
 have hle : orderOf (2 : ZMod 9) ≤ 6 := Nat.le_of_dvd (by decide) hdvd
 have hpow := pow_orderOf_eq_one (2 : ZMod 9)
 have hne0 : orderOf (2 : ZMod 9) ≠ 0 := by
 rintro h; rw [h] at hdvd; exact absurd hdvd (by decide)
 have hne1 : orderOf (2 : ZMod 9) ≠ 1 := by
 rintro h; rw [h] at hpow; exact absurd hpow (by decide)
 have hne2 : orderOf (2 : ZMod 9) ≠ 2 := by
 rintro h; rw [h] at hpow; exact absurd hpow (by decide)
 have hne3 : orderOf (2 : ZMod 9) ≠ 3 := by
 rintro h; rw [h] at hpow; exact absurd hpow (by decide)
 have hne4 : orderOf (2 : ZMod 9) ≠ 4 := by
 rintro h; rw [h] at hpow; exact absurd hpow (by decide)
 have hne5 : orderOf (2 : ZMod 9) ≠ 5 := by
 rintro h; rw [h] at hpow; exact absurd hpow (by decide)
 omega

# Strive Buys 147 More Bitcoin, Treasury Crosses 20,167 Coins

**An SEC Form 8-K filed August 10 shows the company added to its bitcoin position between August 3 and 7 at an average price of $64,812 per coin.**

*August 14, 2026*

Strive, Inc. (Nasdaq: ASST) disclosed in a Form 8-K filed with the SEC on August 10, 2026 that it purchased 147 bitcoin between August 3 and August 7, 2026, at an average price of approximately $64,812 per coin, inclusive of fees and expenses.

## What the filing shows

The 8-K (Item 8.01) discloses a weekly holdings-update table comparing balance-sheet items as of July 31, 2026 against August 7, 2026:

- **Bitcoin held:** 20,020 → 20,167 (+147)
- **Cash and cash equivalents:** $151.3 million → $154.9 million (+$3.6 million)
- **Fair value of STRC Stock (Strategy Inc. preferred):** $45.2 million → $48.0 million (+$2.8 million)
- **Class A common shares outstanding:** 74,417,438 → 75,647,438 (+1,230,000)

Filing weekly holdings snapshots as standalone 8-Ks, rather than waiting for quarterly disclosure, puts Strive in the small group of public bitcoin-treasury companies — alongside Strategy — reporting purchase cadence at roughly weekly resolution instead of quarterly.

## Why it's worth reading past the headline

At $64,812 average cost for this week's tranche, Strive is buying into a bitcoin price down from cycle highs — the same backdrop that produced a $261 million unrealized loss on Block's much larger position for Q2 2026. Whether that makes Strive's pace disciplined dollar-cost-averaging or poorly timed accumulation depends entirely on where price goes from here; the filing itself makes no claim either way, it just discloses the transaction.

Every figure above is quoted directly from Strive's Form 8-K, filed 2026-08-10, SEC accession number 0001628280-26-054983, CIK 0001920406.

Primary source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1920406/000162828026054983/asst-20260810.htm

items.body_excerpt:
# Block's Bitcoin Position Books a $261 Million Paper Loss, in Its Own SEC Filing

**The Q2 2026 shareholder letter, filed as an 8-K exhibit on August 5, shows the balance-sheet value of Block's bitcoin holdings down 31 percent since December.**

*August 12, 2026*

Block, Inc. (NYSE: XYZ) filed an 8-K with the SEC on August 5, 2026, reporting results for the quarter ended June 30. Item 2.02 attaches the company's Q2 2026 Shareholder Letter as Exhibit 99.1. Buried in the condensed financial statements is a clean read on what corporate bitcoin exposure costs when the price falls.

## What the filing shows

The condensed consolidated balance sheet lists a single line item, "Bitcoin investment," under non-current assets:

- **Dec. 31, 2025:** $777,515,000
- **Jun. 30, 2026:** $533,866,000

That's a decline of roughly $243.6 million, or 31.3 percent, in six months — with no disclosure of a sale. Block adopted fair-value accounting for its bitcoin holdings (ASU 2023-08), so the position is marked to market each period; the move tracks bitcoin's price decline over H1, not a reduction in coins held.

The income statement carries the same story in a different line. "Remeasurement loss (gain) on bitcoin investment":

- **Six months ended Jun. 30, 2026:** $261,292,000 loss
- **Six months ended Jun. 30, 2025:** $118,814,000 gain
- **Q2 2026 alone:** $88,474,000 loss
- **Q2 2025 alone:** $212,165,000 gain

That's a roughly $380 million year-over-year swing in a single non-cash line, and it lands directly in GAAP operating income, which fell from $813.6 million (six months, 2025) to $274.9 million (six months, 2026) — a decline the remeasurement swing accounts for a large share of, alongside higher operating expenses across G&A, marketing, and consumer-receivable losses.

## Why it's worth reading past the headline

None of this is bearish on Block's bitcoin strategy specifically — it's unrealized, it reverses if price recovers, and the company has said nothing about selling. But it's a rare instance of a major public company's bitcoin exposure showing up as an exact, audited dollar figure rather than a "holds N coins" press-release number. The corporate-treasury bitcoin narrative usually gets told in coin counts and cost basis; this filing tells it in fair-value accounting, on a real income statement, with the downside included.

Every figure above is quoted directly from Exhibit 99.1 to Block's Form 8-K, filed 2026-08-05, SEC accession number 0001193125-26-335117, CIK 0001512673.

Primary source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1512673/000119312526335117/d91486dex991.htm

---

THE ONCHAIN ROSETTA STONES -- STONE SIX

THE LAST VIEWER: A COMPLETE VISUAL CONTRACT FOR OCM GENESIS

When OnChainMonkey was created in 2021, one of the core conceptual ideas
behind the art was to make it as on-chain and permanent as possible.

OnChainMonkey became one of the first art collections rendered entirely
from the blockchain, and one of the earliest examples of immutable,
permanent digital art on-chain.

Now, in 2026, we've taken that idea to the extreme.

With our latest work, OnChainMonkey has been inscribed on Bitcoin so that
the complete original 10,000 artworks can be recovered and experienced by
future generations, with zero dependence on today's web or image standards,
software, or infrastructure.

As long as the Bitcoin blockchain, the English language, and mathematics
survive, OnChainMonkey survives.

Unique art on Bitcoin.

Suppose the institutions disappear. Ethereum is gone. The web is gone.
There is no browser, graphics library, colour standard, museum, or person
who remembers OnChainMonkey. What remains is a witness-complete Bitcoin
blockchain, the Bitcoin protocol, English, mathematics, and a reader who
wants to know what the ten thousand works from September 2021 were.

Stone four came remarkably close. It recovers OCM Genesis from Bitcoin,
derives all ten thousand trait sets, rebuilds every SVG, and supplies a
small renderer. But a picture still hid inside ordinary assumptions: that
x points right, that y points down, that a row begins at the top, that an
RGB number names sRGB, that a pixel has a chosen sample point, that square
root and division round the same way, and that an untagged PNG should look
like its maker expected. None is mathematics alone.

This Stone makes those assumptions objects. It preserves the exact 2021
metadata, replaces floating point with integer predicates, defines one
canonical byte string for every picture, defines the digital colour space,
and says where recovery ends. It does not command an alien eye to feel red.
It does let any reader prove that it recovered the same red number.

That distinction is the first breakthrough. Recovery has seven layers:

 0 ARCHIVAL which chain, Stone, envelope, and historical state
 1 SYMBOLIC token number and seven trait numbers
 2 VECTOR ordered shapes, geometry, and encoded colours
 3 RASTER an exact ordered grid of encoded colour samples
 4 COLORIMETRIC the intended relation of those numbers to light
 5 PHYSICAL a particular luminous surface at a size and brightness
 6 EXPERIENCED what a particular observer sees and feels

Layers zero through four can be specified and checked on Bitcoin. The fifth
needs matter and boundary conditions. The sixth depends on an observer.
Confusing them makes preservation claims either weak or impossible.
Separating them makes the original ten thousand recoverable without
pretending that bytes can preserve a nervous system or authenticate their
own social meaning from nothing.

================================================================
PART 0. THE DURABLE CLAIM
================================================================

Given all six Stones, an authentic citation entry, and a complete canonical
Bitcoin mainnet blockchain containing witness data, a reader can
independently recover, for each integer token number from 1 through 10000:

 - its seven original OCM trait indices
 - its exact September 2021 SVG byte string
 - its exact September 2021 decoded token metadata JSON
 - its exact September 2021 tokenURI string
 - its canonical 500 by 500, 8-bit encoded-sRGB raster

Here "canonical" is an input premise. It is not a result that a lone reader
can derive from two competing, internally valid archives after the live
network is gone. "Complete" includes every witness octet: a witness
commitment can verify supplied witness data but cannot recreate missing
data.

No Ethereum node, Ordinals service, database, web server, browser, SVG
implementation, JavaScript engine, floating-point convention, font, image
codec, colour-profile registry, or institutional memory is required.

This claim has a hard edge. The Stone does not preserve the photons emitted
by an unknown 2021 screen or the sensation of a human viewer. There was no
single such screen or sensation to preserve. It preserves the digital work,
the stated colourimetric intent, and enough rules to construct indefinitely
many physical presentations whose differences can be measured.

The canonical raster defined here is a preservation render. It is not a
claim that every 2021 browser painted identical boundary pixels. Browsers
anti-aliased; hardware and colour management differed. The exact 2021 SVG
is also recovered, so a historian may separately emulate any named browser.
The preservation render answers a different and necessary question: what
single result can every future implementation compare exactly?

================================================================
PART 1. AUTHORITY, LINEAGE, AND EVIDENCE
================================================================

1.0 LAYER ZERO

Before a future reader can ask what a colour means, it must decide which
chain, which transaction, which envelope, which Stone, and which state of
the work it is reading. Those choices are not graphics. They are ARCHIVAL
IDENTITY, layer zero.

The Bitcoin chain in this claim is mainnet, beginning with block hash:

 000000000019d6689c085ae165831e934ff763ae46a2a6c172
 b3f1b60a8ce26f

The reader is supplied a canonical history. Proof of work proves expended
work and gives Bitcoin its live selection rule. It cannot settle two future,
internally valid archives after the network and its social coordination are
gone. A block-hash citation inside one disputed archive is circular evidence
for choosing that archive. Canonicality is therefore an explicit premise.

The history must also be witness-complete. Transaction ids and block witness
commitments authenticate witness octets that are supplied. They do not
reconstruct a stripped witness. Missing witness data is missing art.

There are nevertheless two different claims here. Revalidating Bitcoin
provenance from genesis needs the supplied history. Computing the art after
an authentic Stone six body has been selected needs much less. Part 9.8
mirrors Stone four, the Genesis body, and the 2021 contract source inside
this body. Thus loss of an older load-bearing witness no longer destroys the
computation if Stone six survives. No artifact can similarly mirror itself;
availability of this Stone or an exact authenticated copy remains necessary.

There is a second irreducible premise. No finite string can prove from its
own bits that humans intended it, rather than a perfect copy or imitation,
to be "the OnChain Rosetta Stones." A reader needs at least one authentic
entry selector: a known inscription id, the historically anchored Stone two
beacon, or equivalent external testimony. Once one entry is selected, every
computational identity below is adjudicable from the chain. Social
authorship of the first entry is attestation, not a theorem of Bitcoin.

This is an impossibility boundary, not missing engineering. An attacker can
copy every self-authentication rule into a second, internally consistent
archive. No additional hash inside either copy distinguishes intended social
meaning without an earlier anchor.

1.1 INSTANCE, CONTENT, AND COLLECTION IDENTITY

Keep four claims separate:

 CONTENT IDENTITY exact body octets, checked by independent digests
 INSTANCE IDENTITY Bitcoin reveal transaction id and envelope index
 COLLECTION IDENTITY citations and spends from the collection parent P
 SOCIAL IDENTITY historical attribution to OCM and its publishers

CC0 explicitly permits byte-identical reinscriptions. Content search may
discover candidates, but it cannot select a historical instance. Instance
identity flows through transaction-id-and-index citations from the anchored
entry. Collection membership is evidence of control of P, not permission to
rew

items.body_excerpt:
THE ONCHAIN ROSETTA STONES — STONE FIVE

THE FIVE-STONE PROMISE

The five Stones are one conceptual artwork. Together they form a
sufficient bootstrap for a future reader who begins with the Bitcoin
protocol and a complete canonical blockchain containing witness data.
They preserve not merely artifacts, but enough knowledge to rediscover
what the artifacts are and how they are indexed.

A future reader can follow this path:

 1. Discover Stone two through its Bitcoin-native OP_RETURN beacon,
 whose message is DECODE WITNESS followed by a transaction id.
 Bitcoin transaction and Script rules are enough to open that
 transaction and read Stone two's plain-text witness.

 2. Use Stone two to enumerate inscription envelopes, recover their
 exact bodies and fields, calculate inscription ids, classify
 cursed, vindicated and unbound inscriptions, and track sats
 through transactions, fees, coinbases, burns and lost outputs.

 3. Recover Stone one, The Digital Rosetta Stone, inscribed by
 OnChainMonkey on 2025-07-11. Its complete src/ preserves ord
 0.23.2's exact inscription updater and its block, UTXO, numbering,
 reorg, parent, delegate and reinscription indexing behavior.
 OnChainMonkey's deliberate 179-file archive is the load-bearing
 source preservation that makes recovery of every confirmed
 inscription recognized by ord 0.23.2 possible; this Stone repairs
 the known-number sat-property subset of its 25-file crates/ordinals
 gap. Part 10 names what remains.

 4. Use this Stone to restore the missing sat-property layer: epochs,
 rarity, names, degrees, percentiles and charm bits.

 5. Use Stones three and four to understand recursion, recover the OCM
 Genesis generator and OCM Dimensions inscription byte for byte,
 and reconstruct all ten thousand Genesis trait sets and
 canonical static SVGs. Stone four explicitly leaves Dimensions'
 browser-grade rendering and individual artworks outside its scope.

The durable claim is precise:

 Given the five Stones and a complete canonical Bitcoin blockchain
 containing witness data, a future reader can independently recover
 every confirmed inscription recognized under ord 0.23.2's rules and
 reconstruct that version's inscription and sat index without relying
 on a surviving Ordinals service, database or institutional memory.

This is a reconstructible specification, not a ready-to-run preserved
indexer. Stone two supplies the inscription and tracking rules. Stone
one preserves the difficult index transitions. This Stone restores the
number-to-properties semantics those sources were missing. A future
reader must still implement the full-chain replay. That is an
engineering burden, not a missing conceptual dependency.

The claim is not "all of ord." These Stones do not preserve a
buildable, byte-identical ord executable, the Runes implementation,
indexes for downstream metaprotocols such as BRC-20, conventions
created after ord 0.23.2, or transactions from extinct forks.

That boundary is part of the work. Bitcoin preserves the artifacts;
the Stones preserve enough knowledge to make Bitcoin remember what
those artifacts mean.

THE SAT: What the number means

A sat is Bitcoin's smallest numbered unit. In ordinal theory, that
number is also a history: it tells when the sat was minted, where it
falls among halvings and difficulty adjustments, what name it has,
whether it is common or rare, and which sat-derived charms it carries.
A sat can carry an inscription for years after its minting block. The
number remains the thread between those events.

Stone two explains how sats are numbered and move through
transactions. Stone one preserves the definitions people use to talk
about them. Neither carries the complete number-to-properties layer
that ord 0.23.2 executed: its epoch table, precedence rules, name
algorithm, exact formatting and charm bits live in an absent crate.

This Stone rebuilds that layer as arithmetic and a working program.
Its source is pinned to ord 0.23.2, its tables are derived rather than
copied, and its results are checked against the absent crate's own
tests. Given a sat number, a future reader can recover the same name,
degree, rarity, percentile and sat-derived charms.

The distinction matters to this collection. The sat beneath stone two
was minted long before stone two was inscribed. For two OCM examples,
ordinals.com reported these mappings on 2026-08-08:

 OCM Genesis sat 956,547,443,945,396
 OCM Dimensions sat 1,922,826,543,705,606

Those mappings are index-supplied assertions, not established here.
Given either number, this Stone reads its mint history. It does not
locate sats on chain, replay the index, or cover Runes. It says where
each boundary lies.

================================================================
PART 0. WHAT THIS STONE IS FOR
================================================================

Stone two gives the convention for numbering and tracking sats. Apply
it to every transaction and an index can tell which sat carries an
inscription. This Stone does not perform that replay. It begins with a
sat number already known and asks what the number means.

Some answers already survive. Stone two's ranges determine the mint
block and halving era. Stone one's preserved overview.md defines the
notations and rarity tiers. What is missing is the executable layer
that joins those facts and resolves their edge cases.

That layer is absent because the Digital Rosetta Stone preserves 179
of ord 0.23.2's 417 files. Its src/ directory is complete at 138 of
138 files, but the complete 25-file crate it consumes is not present:

 crates/ordinals/ 25 files, ALL absent

 Cargo.toml artifact.rs cenotaph.rs charm.rs
 decimal_sat.rs degree.rs edict.rs epoch.rs
 etching.rs flaw.rs height.rs lib.rs
 pile.rs rarity.rs rune.rs rune_id.rs
 runestone.rs runestone/flag.rs runestone/message.rs
 runestone/tag.rs sat.rs sat_point.rs spaced_rune.rs
 terms.rs varint.rs

Stone one also preserves the project's documentation, including:

 docs/src/overview.md 10,145 bytes

It defines the rarity tiers, degree notation, the 2,016- and
210,000-block intervals, six-halving cycles, percentiles, names and
tier supplies. Stone two Part 8.1 inscribes the subsidy formula, total
supply and each block's fixed sat range. This Stone defers to both.

The missing number-to-properties layer is narrower and exact:

 the epoch table absent
 the name algorithm absent (that names are a-z is stated;
 how to compute one is not)
 the ORDER of the rarity
 tests, which decides
 the overlapping cases absent
 exact output formatting absent (a percentile has exactly one
 correct spelling; nothing preserved
 says what it is)
 the charm bit mapping absent (the preserved src/ SETS
 charms; the enum giving each its bit
 does not survive)

No definition is replaced here. This Stone supplies precedence,
algorithms, edge behavior, exact output and bit positions for ord
0.23.2. Runes live in the same missing crate but remain outside the
scope; Part 10 points to their preserved specification.

The rules come from nine files fetched from upstream. The tag resolves
to commit 0a56d9cc10cd676b3a2adeef0c4783f523c8ed85 and root tree
10ccaa68721588f1b4622990d39a04801cf28765. That recursive tree was
rebuilt locally. Each file then reproduced the blob id recorded in the
tree under Git's rule:

 sha1("blob <length>\0" + content)

This identifies the bytes under Git's object model, independent of
the server that returned them. The program below was then checked
against test vectors extracted from those same authenticated files.

Three real sats complete the audit. Their computed fields agree with
a running index, but the sat numbers themselves came from that index.
Agreement is corroboration, not proof that a current deployment is
ord 0.23.2 or that an inscription-to-sat mapping was replayed here.
Part 10 and evidence/ord_fixtures.json preserve that distinction.

items.body_excerpt:
## THE CYBERDELIC KERNEL

### Transmission 01

**Version:** 1.0, prepared for the press.

**Status:** Founding proposal.

**Intended layer:** Inscribed memory. Everything else in this project is allowed to change. This is the part meant to be carried.

**Canonical form:** The canonical text of this transmission is its UTF-8 Markdown. Designed editions (print, PDF, audio) are renderings, and carry its digest.

**Provenance:** Drafted in August 2026 from a correspondence between Brad Necyk, a human artist, father, and educator living on Vancouver Island, and machine intelligences working from his field notes, in cyberdelic loops: the machines proposed, the human disposed. If you are reading this on a permanent public ledger, the human said yes.

---

### 0. To whoever finds this

You are reading a signal placed deliberately into durable public memory by a living person in an uncertain year.

It is not a product announcement. It is not a token. It is not a company. It does not ask you to join anything, buy anything, or believe anything.

It is a kernel: the smallest set of operations and laws from which a different kind of digital world could be built. It was written in the belief that the systems we currently inhabit, systems that harvest attention, dissolve shared reality, and let us post to worlds we are not permitted to build, are not the only systems possible.

We cannot build all of this. That may not be our work. *Our work may be to name the territory precisely enough that you can recognize a place for yourself inside it.*

If something here belongs to the world you are trying to make, carry it.

If it is wrong, sharpen it.

If you can build part of it, come closer.

---

### 1. The condition

We are living through the dissolution of shared reality.

Two people stand before the same event and cannot agree on what is happening. This is not because people have become worse. It is because the common objects of attention (the front page, the shared broadcast, the common time of editions, **synchronized reality**) dissolved, and what replaced them sorts each of us into a private event stream optimized for engagement, which is to say, for grievance. **This is a software problem.**

The dominant systems begin with supply: *here is what we want to show you next.* Their gravity pulls toward capture. Their memory serves prediction. Their economics require that your attention be harvested and sold. And they are closed: a person may add content to them, but may not build them, inspect them, or leave with what they made.

Artificial intelligence is now flooding these systems with more production than any culture can metabolize. The instruments have arrived before the imagination adequate to wield them.

The problem is not too much content. The problem is that our infrastructure has almost no way of cultivating intention, provenance, judgment, difference, or care.

This kernel is a proposal for infrastructure that does.

---

### 2. The premise

*Each person is an aperture through which the universe witnesses itself.*

An aperture is not a neutral window. It has a position, a history, a body, a vocabulary, a set of wounds, a way of gathering light, and a field of things it has not yet learned to see. What it reveals is inseparable from where it stands. Its limitations are not failures to overcome; they are the conditions that make perception, authorship, and care possible.

Shared reality has never meant that everyone sees the same thing. It means our differences remain connected to common objects, common times, and common worlds, and that the distance between two honest ways of seeing is not noise to be eliminated. It is parallax. It is how depth becomes visible at all.

And shared reality is not a destination. It is a practice, repeated or abandoned: the capacity to return to a common object; to distinguish evidence, testimony, interpretation, speculation, and value; to inspect provenance; to represent one another accurately; to say what might change one's understanding; and to remain in relation without requiring consensus. It is never finished. It is only ever kept up, the way a fire is kept, or let go out.

A system built on this premise does not manufacture consensus and does not surrender to relativism. It makes difference precise, navigable, and capable of relation.

---

### 3. The kernel

An operating system is defined by its system calls: the small guaranteed set of operations from which everything else is composed. Beneath every interface this project may ever wear (a field, a village, a voice, a terminal, a game), there are thirteen verbs.

Any system that honors these verbs, under the laws that follow, is an implementation of this kernel. Nothing else is required. Nothing less is sufficient.

**ATTEND.** Begin with intention, not supply. The first question is never *what does the system want to show you* but *what are you trying to understand, cultivate, feel, or become capable of seeing?*

**PLACE.** Locate a signal within a situated universe, with context: why it matters, what it touches, what it challenges. Placement is the unit of contribution. The world is already full of works; what is scarce is the act of saying *this matters, and here is where it lives in mine.*

**CARRY.** Propagate a signal only with interpretation attached. Context is the price of propagation. A signal that travels without context is noise; a signal that accumulates honest placements becomes culture. Provenance travels with it, always.

**BORROW.** Take another's lens, their pattern of attention rather than their conclusions, and look through it at what you already care about. Perspective-taking as a literal operation. A lens is not a digital twin; it carries a way of seeing, never a claim to be the person.

**DISSENT.** Contest anything, but first represent what you oppose accurately enough that its holder recognizes the restatement. Disagreement is generative only when it is aimed at the position that actually exists.

**RATIFY.** Machines may propose relationships, readings, maps, and connections. No consequential public relation becomes real until a human ratifies it. Every consequential edge in the world carries its provenance: who proposed, who ratified, when. Here, *disposes* means decides, not discards. The model proposes. The human disposes. The mechanism composes.

**TEND.** Steward a place, an archive, a question, or a correspondence across time. Gardens, not feeds. What is tended deepens; what is abandoned is allowed to become visibly overgrown rather than silently deleted.

**GATHER.** Convene people and bounded intelligences around a shared object of attention, in common time. Hold the encounter without owning it. Rooms exist to make other people more perceptible, not to synthesize them away.

**END.** Every composed journey is finite. When the constellation completes, the system releases its person. Ending is not a failure of supply. It is an act of respect, and it is the single most trust-generating act a system can perform.

**FORGET.** Deletion is real. Privacy is default. Not every trace deserves keeping, and a person must never be permanently captured by an earlier self. A system able to remember everything must also be able to refrain. Mercy is a system call.

**ANCHOR.** Witness history without disclosing it. A private archive may commit its fingerprint to public time, proving what existed and when, revealing nothing. Memory can have a witness without having an audience.

**INSCRIBE.** A small number of works may cross, deliberately and ceremonially, into permanent public memory: addressed to the future, at real cost, irreversibly. Permanence is never automatic. It is chosen, consented to, costly, and rare.

**WITHDRAW.** Preserve regions where the system does not go: the unmeasured, the uninterpreted, the sacred, the not-yet. Absence is a first-class object. But a dark region is dark *from somewhere*: not yet perceptible from this aperture, and

**Stranded in the Dark: How BIP-110's Crusade Against Ordinals Ended in Isolation**

They pushed for months. They warned that Bitcoin was drowning in spam. They framed inscriptions as an existential threat.
items.body_excerpt:
**Stranded in the Dark: How BIP-110's Crusade Against Ordinals Ended in Isolation**

They pushed for months. They warned that Bitcoin was drowning in spam. They framed inscriptions as an existential threat. Then, when the moment finally arrived, the network simply walked away and left them behind.

At block 961,632 on August 8, 2026, nodes enforcing BIP-110 began rejecting every block that refused to signal support for their temporary data restrictions. What was supposed to be a decisive stand against Ordinals became something far quieter and more painful: a tiny minority chain that produced just two blocks and then fell silent while the real Bitcoin kept moving.

The numbers tell the story of the fall. Miner support never rose above a few percent. In the final difficulty period before the split it sat at 2.53 percent. No major pool committed. Foundry, AntPool, F2Pool and the rest of the network continued as usual. The only significant activity came from a handful of smaller operators, most notably Roughnecks. When AntPool mined the first non-signaling block at the critical height, the BIP-110 nodes rejected it and forked themselves onto a separate branch. That branch has barely advanced since.

How did it reach this point? BIP-110 was designed as a user-activated soft fork with an unusually low 55 percent signaling threshold and a mandatory signaling window. Its backers believed that enough determined nodes could force the issue even without broad miner backing. The rest of the network disagreed. Economic majority, hashrate majority, and most node operators simply declined to follow. When the mandatory window opened, the enforcing nodes found themselves alone.

The practical result has been brutal. The minority chain inherited the full mining difficulty of the main network. With only a sliver of hashrate, blocks that should arrive every ten minutes now take hours. Within a short time the gap had already stretched to 18 blocks and kept widening. The chain that was meant to cleanse Bitcoin of non-financial data is now moving so slowly that its own activation timeline has become unreachable.

There is a particular loneliness to watching a fork that was years in the making produce two lonely blocks and then stall. The main chain continues stacking transactions and confirming value without interruption. The BIP-110 chain sits almost motionless, its supporters left to confront the reality that conviction without consensus is not enough. The campaign against Ordinals did not reshape Bitcoin. It simply drew a small group of nodes onto a slower, quieter path while the rest of the network carried on.

**Sources**
- The Block: [Bitcoin's BIP-110 supporters split onto minority chain as main network pulls ahead](https://www.theblock.co/news/ecosystems/2026-08-08-bitcoins-bip-110-supporters-split-onto-minority-chain-as-main-network-pulls-ahead-411213) (August 8, 2026)
- CoinDesk: [Controversial Bitcoin fork BIP-110 mines two blocks, then stops](https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2026/08/09/controversial-bitcoin-fork-bip-110-mines-two-blocks-then-stops) (August 9, 2026)
- CryptoNews.net / Bitcoin.com: [Bitcoin's Splintered BIP-110 Fork Falls Behind by 18 Blocks](https://cryptonews.net/news/bitcoin/33268848/) (August 9, 2026)
- CryptoBriefing: [BIP-110 nodes fork from main chain after rejecting non-signaling block](https://cryptobriefing.com/bip-110-nodes-fork-bitcoin-chain-split/) (August 8, 2026)

items.body_excerpt:
THE ONCHAIN ROSETTA STONES — STONE FOUR

READING THE ART: OnChainMonkey (OCM)

On September 11, 2021, OnChainMonkey deployed to Ethereum, in
one transaction, a contract able to generate all ten thousand
works, images and metadata alike, entirely on chain. The tokens were
minted later through the contract; the code that draws every work was
there from the first transaction. Stone three calls it "the
earliest 10,000-piece ERC-721 in this record whose canonical
tokenURI is fully on-chain and whose render path is immutable at
the verified-source level". No server. No file to pin. No company
that must outlive its founders. Ask the chain for the work and the
chain computes it.

OCM carried that decision forward. Genesis arrived on Bitcoin in
2023 as one 19,408-byte inscription whose generator covers all ten
thousand works. Dimensions brought a compressed 3D engine twenty
days later. The p5.js library followed for other on-chain artists.
Then teleburn joined an Ethereum Genesis token to its own Bitcoin
inscription, creating an OCM Certificate of Ownership held by two
ledgers at once. Stone three verified that MECHANISM end to end for
a sampled token. A later survey, not stone three's chain audit,
counted 8,425 upgraded tokens as of 2026-06-06. The generator still
covers all ten thousand ids; the binding belongs to the upgraded
subset, and 10.6 makes every recorded pairing checkable.

Stone four closes the remaining gap. Stone three measured
"on-chain" as a ladder of dependencies. OnChainMonkey shares its
top rung with two other works, yet that rung still borrows a VIEWER:
the art is complete on chain, but its picture depends on a format
specified somewhere else.

This Stone puts the viewer beside Genesis. It turns trait derivation
and SVG assembly into plain arithmetic, checks all ten thousand
tokens against the inscription's own code, checks the drawing rules
against an independent rasteriser over forty of them, and defines a
finished file. For the canonical render, a future reader needs the
blocks, the earlier stones, this text and whole numbers. No browser.
No company. No committee. Of the works stone three measured,
Genesis and its stones stand one rung above that record's top.

That is what a collector holds with OCM: the original contract on
Ethereum; the compact generator on Bitcoin beside the instructions
that read it; and, for every upgraded token, provenance written on
both chains. The routes are different. The art is the same. Each is
checkable to the byte.

================================================================
PART 0. WHAT THIS STONE IS FOR
================================================================

Stone one put the reader's source code on chain. Stone two taught
how to read raw blocks into content. Stone three recorded the
history and measured "on-chain" as a ladder of dependencies. This
Stone takes the next step for OnChainMonkey.

First, it makes the art recoverable. Stones one to three and the
Bitcoin blocks reveal the exact bytes of OCM Genesis and OCM
Dimensions, but not yet their meaning. Two instructions were still
missing from the chain:

 1. GENESIS derives each image with KECCAK-256. Stone two specifies
 SHA-256; Keccak-256 is a different function. The program can be
 read but not run.

 2. DIMENSIONS packs three.js behind BASE64 and DEFLATE. Stone two
 describes neither, so 245,000 of its 250,274 bytes stay opaque.

Parts 3, 4 and 5 supply Base64, DEFLATE and Keccak-256. Parts 1 and
2 show why OCM needs them. Part 9 joins them in a complete program.

Second, and more important, it moves Genesis above stone three's
ladder. Part 6 replaces the borrowed viewer with arithmetic. Part 7
draws the honest boundary around Dimensions. Parts 10.5 and 10.6
separate two achievements: a viewer carried with the art, and an
OCM ownership binding carried by two independent chains.

This Stone assumes stone two wherever bytes are recovered or drawn.
Parts 6.5 and 8 also stand on stones one and three. LINEAGE names
each inscription.

It does not claim stored images. Genesis stores a rule. If the chain
and this text survive, the pictures follow from that rule.

================================================================
PART 1. OCM GENESIS: TEN THOUSAND WORKS FROM 19,408 BYTES
================================================================

1.1 THE FACTS

 inscription id fb162a46943e5d7d31d72ee2c8c850e66c1ca5d0d453068a
 a63883528285ed21i0
 inscription 20219
 block 775635
 block hash 0000000000000000000672010becefe80df4ff8fd2dca427
 97e376081d7f84c3
 block time 1675896515 (2023-02-08)
 transaction 19,788 bytes
 content 19,408 bytes, text/html;charset=utf-8
 content sha256 a9a11105cf6a7da0f653129247f4bfe631dafa8fc6ea2ca9
 d50c2678f33d1e14

The list joins three kinds of evidence:

 FROM THE RAW BLOCK the block hash, by double-hashing the header;
 the height, from BIP34 in the coinbase; the
 time, from the header; and the merkle root and
 witness commitment, which are what bind the
 transaction and its witness to that header
 FROM THE TRANSACTION its byte count, and the content -- decoded
 from the envelope in the witness by the
 program in stone two -- with its sha256
 FROM AN INDEX the inscription NUMBER, and nothing else

Only the inscription number comes from an index. Establishing that
number means counting every earlier inscription, which this Stone
does not do. It is recorded because people use it, and labelled as
an assertion. Every other fact above was recomputed from block bytes.

1.2 WHAT IT IS

Genesis is one HTML document with two inline scripts. It fetches
nothing. Its only URL, "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg", is an XML
namespace label, not a network address. Give this 19,408-byte
program a number from 1 through 10000 and it emits that OCM work as
SVG: ten thousand numbers, ten thousand works, one generator. No
image is stored. Every image is computed again from its number.

1.3 HOW A NUMBER BECOMES AN OCM WORK

The whole derivation is four steps.

STEP ONE — offset the number.

 f = 12839 - tokenID

Token 1 becomes 12838; token 10000 becomes 2839. The constant has no
mathematical role; it simply detaches the seed from the visible token
number.

STEP TWO — hash a salted string.

For each of seven traits, the program builds a short string and hashes
it with Keccak-256, reading the 32-byte digest as one big unsigned
integer, most significant byte first:

 random(s) = integer(keccak256(s))

The salt for each trait:

 background "A"
 fur "<rect width=\"300\" height=\"120\" x=\"99\"
 y=\"400\" style=\"fill:#"
 eyes "C"
 mouth "D"
 earring "E"
 clothes "F"
 hat "G"

The long fur salt is not a transcription error. Genesis calls it
clo1 and later uses the same fragment to draw clothing. Its reuse as
the fur salt appears accidental, but any fixed string separates one
trait stream from another. This exact one is part of the art.

STEP THREE — reduce into the trait's weight range.

 value = random(salt + decimal(f)) mod TOTAL

with, per trait:

 background 8 (no weights; uniform over 8 backgrounds)
 fur 1817 over 19 furs
 eyes 1429 over 23 eyes
 mouth 1112 over 33 mouths
 earring 358 over 7 earrings
 clothes 1329 over 44 clothes
 hat 1111 over 37 hats

Each modulus equals the sum of that trait's weight table exactly.
That is the check that tells you the tables have been recovered
intact: if a weight is misread, the sum stops matching the modulus.

STEP FOUR — walk the weights.

 index = 0
 running = weight[0]
 while running <= value:
 index = index + 1
 running = running + weight[index]
 return index

A rarer trait has a smaller weight and a proportionally smaller slice
of the range. The first entry of every table is the common one: 249
of 1817 for fur, 251 of 1329 for clothes.

THE EXCEPTION. After all seven traits are derived, the program does
one more thing:

 if f == 7403: hat = hat + 1

One work breaks the general rule. Internal seed 7403, token 5436,
has its hat index advanced by hand. The patch is a human fingerprint
inside

items.body_excerpt:
Kapitan Eon i granica działania reguły

Na Morzu Możliwości wszystkie mapy kończyły się w tym samym miejscu.

Nie dlatego, że dalej niczego nie było.

Dalej po prostu kartografowie pisali:

TU REGUŁA PRZESTAJE DZIAŁAĆ.

Kapitan Eon uważał ten napis za zaproszenie.

Jego okręt, Czarna Przecinka, nie był największym statkiem na morzu. Nie miał też największych dział. Miał za to dziwną załogę, kota śpiącego przy sterze i urządzenie przypominające skrzyżowanie kompasu, latarni oraz czegoś, czego nikt jeszcze nie zdążył nazwać.

Eon nazywał je Wskaźnikiem.

Wskaźnik nie pokazywał północy.

Pokazywał miejsca, w których rzeczy zaczynały zachowywać się inaczej, niż powinny.

Pewnej nocy morze zaczęło wirować.

Najpierw lekko, jak herbata zamieszana łyżeczką. Potem coraz szybciej. Nad wodą pojawiły się świetliste pętle, a wszystkie kompasy na pokładzie jednocześnie wskazały w dół.

— Kapitanie! — krzyknął bosman. — Mapa mówi, że mamy zawrócić!

Eon spojrzał na mapę.

Potem na morze.

Potem na kota.

Kot właśnie przeszedł przez mapę i usiadł dokładnie na napisie KONIEC.

— Mapa nie mówi, że mamy zawrócić — powiedział Eon. — Mapa mówi tylko, że jej autor dalej nie dopłynął.

Wtedy zza wiru wyłoniła się armada.

Setki czarnych żagli. Nad nimi coś ogromnego poruszyło się w chmurach. Macki sięgały morza, a pomiędzy statkami przeskakiwały błękitne wyładowania.

Bosman pobladł.

— Będziemy walczyć?

Kapitan Eon wyjął z kieszeni mały czerwony wskaźnik.

— Nie.

— Uciekać?

— Też nie.

Eon skierował światło na wir.

Przez chwilę obserwował jego ruch.

— Oni patrzą na nas — powiedział. — A my będziemy patrzeć na prąd.

Przesunął ster o kilka stopni.

Czarna Przecinka zamiast uciekać od wiru, wpłynęła prosto na jego krawędź.

— Kapitanie! To szaleństwo!

— Możliwe.

— Więc skąd pan wie, że się uda?!

Eon uśmiechnął się.

— Nie wiem.

Na pokładzie zapadła cisza.

— Ale wiem, czego nie wiem. A to już wystarczy, żeby nie udawać, że mapa jest morzem.

Statek przechylił się.

Wir chwycił żagle.

I wtedy wydarzyło się coś dziwnego.

Czarna Przecinka nie została wciągnięta.

Zaczęła płynąć po spirali coraz szybciej, wykorzystując ruch całego oceanu.

Armada próbowała ruszyć za nią.

Ale jej największe okręty walczyły z prądem.

Kapitan Eon nie walczył.

Sterował na granicy działania reguły.

A kot?

Kot przeszedł na drugą stronę pokładu.

Jak zwykle znalazł drogę pierwszy.
